clue.text: Farewell is written inside bag

indicators.note: something written inside sits within the outer word, so the short piece goes into the middle of the other

parts.note: Latin goodbye, used in English as a formal farewell

explanation.surface: A goodbye note has been tucked inside someone's luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: Vale is the Latin farewell, still used in formal English goodbyes and epitaphs.
explanation.definitionFit: A valise is a small travelling case for clothes, a kind of luggage carried by hand.

clue.text: Diligence required for gathering plums

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a diligence was a horse-drawn coach, and so is this light carriage

definitions.note: describes a plum variety, not a noun
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the name of a popular English plum variety, which pickers gather

explanation.walkthrough: 'Diligence' looks like hard work; it is an old public stagecoach, standing in for another horse-drawn carriage. The plum half is loose: Victoria is the commonest English plum, but 'required for gathering' is not fully explained.
explanation.definitionFit: A victoria is a low four-wheeled carriage, and it is also a well-known variety of English dessert plum.

clue.text: The burning question of bouncing babies

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a topical matter still being hotly debated

explanation.walkthrough: Issue means both a matter for debate and children; live means current and also alive.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic of current debate is a live issue, and healthy children are, literally, issue that is alive.

clue.text: Purely male speculator

definitions.meaning: first meaning: men only, as in a party before a wedding
second meaning: a stock-market buyer of new shares hoping to sell quickly for profit

explanation.walkthrough: A stag party is a British bachelor party; in City slang a stag applies for new share issues to resell at once.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective use means for men only, and the noun is stock-exchange slang for a quick-profit share applicant.

clue.text: Profit alleged to be disputed

parts.note: something alleged is said to be so

explanation.surface: A claimed profit is being challenged, as in a business dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: To gainsay is to contradict or deny, so a claim that was gainsaid was argued against.

clue.text: One is able in this way to plant

explanation.surface: Instructions saying anyone capable may plant something this way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a verb about gardening; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Acanthus is a Mediterranean flowering perennial whose leaves inspired Corinthian column decoration.

clue.text: Football then is unfair

definitions.meaning: first meaning, taken literally: football is a game that is a different sport from cricket
second meaning: the British idiom for unsporting conduct

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket is the British byword for fair play, so 'not cricket' means not done.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes dishonourable behaviour, and football literally is a sport other than cricket.

clue.text: Imitating sound of a bullet

parts.note: the ringing noise a bullet makes striking metal

explanation.surface: Mimicking the noise of a gunshot.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue order is reversed: 'a' comes before the bullet's sound in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to copy them, so aping means mimicking.

clue.text: I would return instrument much weakened

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way one came, so these letters are read backwards

parts.note: a lute is a stringed instrument

explanation.surface: Someone would take back a badly damaged instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: To dilute is to thin a liquid by adding water, greatly reducing its strength.

clue.text: Gone a curious way for a cake

indicators.note: arranged in a curious way means put in an odd, unexpected order

explanation.surface: A cake has vanished by some strange route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone a' reads like part of a sentence about leaving; the two words are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Genoa cake is a rich British fruit cake topped with almonds.

clue.text: "Twas —— to the general" (Hamlet)

parts.note: a line from Hamlet with one word blanked out
the source tells the solver to recall the play: the general public did not appreciate a refined delicacy

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation fill-in: Hamlet says a play 'pleased not the million; 'twas caviare to the general', meaning too refined for ordinary people. CAVIARE is the old spelling of caviar.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Shakespeare's line is the fish-roe delicacy, used figuratively for something too refined for popular taste.

clue.text: To which workers swarm to make their pile

definitions.text: To which workers swarm to make their pile

parts.words: To which workers swarm to make their pile
parts.note: surface reading: labourers crowding to a site where they make their fortune
setter's reading: worker insects swarming over the heap they build

explanation.walkthrough: 'Workers' and 'make their pile' suggest people chasing a fortune; worker insects actually build a heaped nest of earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Worker ants build and swarm over a mound of soil, which is literally a pile they have made.

clue.text: No part has died

parts.note: nought, a zero, stands for none

explanation.surface: A statement that nothing at all has perished.
explanation.walkthrough: OBIT is Latin for 'died', seen on gravestones and old records.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin verb form found on memorial inscriptions means the person passed away on the given date.

clue.text: River just for Frank

parts.note: the Forth is a Scottish river
just in the sense of fair and correct

explanation.surface: A river named after a man called Frank, as if fairness were on the waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a man's name; it is the adjective meaning candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone open and direct who speaks plainly without evasion.

clue.text: Game to cook two kinds of bacon

wordplay.note: back bacon and gammon are two different cuts of cured pork

explanation.surface: A recipe calling for two sorts of bacon to be cooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like meat to be cooked; it is the board game. Back is the lean bacon cut; gammon is cured ham from the hind leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Backgammon is a board game for two players moving counters by dice.

clue.text: Set up this month with a pound

parts.note: inst., short for instant, is the old business-letter abbreviation for the current month
L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound

explanation.surface: Something is being established this month, costing a pound.
explanation.definitionFit: To instal (older British spelling) is to put equipment in place ready for use, which is setting it up.

clue.text: Fight increase in cost of magazine

parts.note: Punch was a famous British humour magazine

explanation.surface: A row breaks out because a magazine has put up its price.
explanation.walkthrough: The magazine's name comes first though the clue mentions it last: Punch up, its price raised.
explanation.definitionFit: A punch-up is British slang for a brawl or fist fight.

clue.text: Out of bed and at a pinch wide awake

parts.note: someone out of bed is up
snuff is powdered tobacco taken by the pinch

explanation.surface: Someone who is up and, if need be, fully alert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At a pinch' looks like 'if necessary'; snuff is taken a pinch at a time. The 'to' is only loosely clued by 'at'.
explanation.definitionFit: Up to snuff is an idiom meaning sharp and not easily fooled, so fully alert.

clue.text: Churchman in the red

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a senior Roman Catholic prelate
second meaning: a deep scarlet shade

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a cleric in debt or dressed in scarlet; cardinals do wear red.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardinal is a high-ranking Catholic prelate, and cardinal is also the name of a vivid scarlet colour.

clue.text: It's useless for ambitious PC to be tired

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a police round where nothing happens, no use to a constable seeking arrests

explanation.walkthrough: A PC is a police constable, whose patrol route is his beat; a dead one offers no chance to shine. Dead beat is also British for worn out.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead beat is an idiom for utterly exhausted, and punningly a lifeless patrol route for a constable.

clue.text: Nibble at meat in London

definitions.note: the definition names a place found in London

parts.note: to peck at food is to nibble it

explanation.surface: Someone picks at a plate of meat somewhere in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Peckham is a district of south-east London.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a neighbourhood located within the British capital, so it is a place in that city.

clue.text: Place Peg on seat

parts.note: a tee is the small peg a golf ball rests on

explanation.surface: An instruction to sit a woman called Peg on a chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peg' looks like a woman's name; it is the golfer's tee.
explanation.definitionFit: A settee is an upholstered sofa for more than one person, so it is a kind of seat.

clue.text: Frame up for Count to take sailor and airman to America

definitions.note: a frame set up for counting

parts.note: AC, aircraftman, the lowest RAF rank

explanation.surface: An aristocrat is framed and must take a sailor and an airman to America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a nobleman; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame of beads on wires used for doing arithmetic by hand.

clue.text: Mischief science does to a member

explanation.surface: Science inflicting harm on a member of some body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' looks like a limb; it is a Member of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: A mischievous child is called 'a little mischief' or a rascal, the same sense as a playful rogue.

clue.text: Missile certainly has to get out of way of fish

parts.note: to duck is to dodge out of the way

explanation.surface: Someone must dodge an incoming missile, as if under fire.
explanation.walkthrough: Bombay duck is not a bird: it is a small dried fish eaten in South Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombay duck is the name of the lizardfish, dried and salted, despite its bird-like name.

clue.text: Man of resolution takes thousand across

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
to go across is to go over

explanation.surface: A determined man carries a thousand across somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resolution' looks like determination; it is a motion put to a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: At a meeting the person who formally proposes a motion or resolution is called its proposer.

clue.text: Employed by transatlantic editor

parts.note: across the Atlantic from Britain is the United States

explanation.surface: Someone works for an American newspaper editor.
explanation.definitionFit: Something employed has been put to use, made use of for a purpose.

clue.text: Daughter has spot of bother with skirting

explanation.surface: A daughter in a bit of trouble over a skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirting' looks like a garment or avoidance; it is skirting board.
explanation.definitionFit: A dado is the lower panelled part of an interior wall, like a skirting board.

clue.text: Primitive type is on the look-out …

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a prehistoric human who lived in caves

definitions.note: describes the keeper of 'cave', not a noun
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a schoolboy keeping 'cave' (Latin, beware) watches out for masters

explanation.surface: A primitive person keeps watch, as the ellipsis leads into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: In British school slang to 'keep cave' (Latin, beware) was to stand lookout and call a warning when a master came, so the boy on the look-out is a cave man.
explanation.definitionFit: A caveman is a stone-age human, and also, punningly, the boy posted to cry the Latin warning word.

clue.text: … for me to a certain degree

explanation.surface: It continues the previous clue: the lookout is watching out for me, to some extent.
explanation.definitionFit: A measure is an amount or extent, as in 'a measure of success', so it means a degree.

clue.text: Choke by the way applied right on corner

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Someone is throttled in the street, cornered by an attacker.
explanation.definitionFit: To strangle is to throttle by squeezing the throat, which is to choke someone.

clue.text: Sweet to take care of Frenchman so well

parts.note: c/o is the postal abbreviation for care of
M., for monsieur, is the French title for a man

explanation.surface: Looking after a Frenchman so well that it seems sweet of you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like an adjective praising kindness; it is the noun for a confection.
explanation.definitionFit: A comfit is a sugar-coated seed or nut, an old-fashioned confection.
